description: We are a team of four students from Nanyang Technological University (NTU), Singapore, passionate about AI, software development, data science, and sustainability. For NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, we are building AgriShift, a climate-smart agricultural planning platform using NASA Earth observation data to compare crop rotation strategies, assess water and climate risks, and support sustainable farming decisions.
summary: AgriShift is a field-level decision tool that helps irrigated farmers on the High Plains choose crop rotations that protect water, soil and income before they plant. A farmer selects a field. AgriShift detects the current rotation from USDA crop maps and asks up to 7 optional questions about goals, equipment and markets. It then simulates 9 rotations against 42 seasons of NASA POWER weather (1985–2025), using FAO-56 crop water use and FAO-33 yield response. Each rotation gets a 0–100 score for water, soil, income and climate risk, and comes with its reasons, data gaps and what to check locally. Our case study is the Sheridan 6 LEMA in northwest Kansas, where farmers agreed in 2013 to cap groundwater pumping at 11 in/yr. In a back-test using only data up to 2012, AgriShift favours wheat and sorghum, the direction Sheridan 6 moved. The High Plains aquifer supplies about 30% of US irrigation groundwater and is declining. Farmers need a transparent way to adapt, not a black box.
details:
What it does: AgriShift compares complete crop rotations for one field. Existing tools cover isolated tasks: irrigation scheduling for a crop already chosen, farm records, or cover-crop picks.

  1. Know: detects the field’s current rotation (USDA Cropland Data Layer) and scores it.
  2. Ask: 7 quick, skippable questions: priorities (water, soil, income, resilience), equipment, buyers and soil pH.
  3. Compare: simulates 9 rotations across 42 seasons under the farm’s pumping cap, grouped into weather types (hot & dry, typical, wet, cool & wet). Shows water pumped, average margin, margin in hot, dry years, nitrogen need and bare-soil months against the current rotation.
  4. Decide: each recommendation explains why it ranks where it does, the evidence behind it, data gaps and local checks (well capacity, elevator, soil test, K-State Extension).
  5. Prove: a back-test using only data up to 2012, checked against what Sheridan 6 farmers did after the 2013 cap.

How it works: daily NASA POWER weather (blended with ERA5) drives FAO-56 crop evapotranspiration (Kc × ET0) and FAO-33 yield response to water stress. Economics use USDA NASS prices and K-State budget defaults, which the farmer can edit. k-means clustering groups seasons into weather types for risk. Scores are weighted by the farmer’s own priorities, and rotations are ruled out when equipment, markets or soil pH don’t fit.

Benefits and impact: farmers see water savings and income side by side before they commit. For the Sheridan 6 demo field, wheat -> sorghum pumps less than the current corn-heavy rotation and turns a −$17/ac average margin into +$72/ac. Every recommendation is honest about its uncertainty.

Tools: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre and Express 5 (Node.js), sql.js/PostgreSQL, and Electron for desktop. Deployed on Vercel.

Creativity and factors considered: the back-test is an out-of-sample “time machine” check. Every output states its assumptions, gaps and local checks, and every citation is automatically checked against a registry of real papers. We considered farmer autonomy (all inputs editable and skippable), real constraints (pumping caps, equipment, markets), soil health, climate risk and transparency.
dataRefs: NASA POWER (Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources) daily agroclimatology data
